audience_one_line: An Indian retail or HNI applicant who has bid in a mainboard IPO and wants to understand exactly how the shares are carved between QIB, anchor, NII, retail, employee and shareholder buckets — and why retail allotment in an oversubscribed issue is a lottery, not a market.
must_answer: What is the headline allocation between QIB / NII / retail in a normal book-built IPO, and how does it change when the issuer is a loss-making company required to do a compulsory-QIB book?
How is the anchor investor portion carved out of the QIB book — what is the cap, the minimum ticket, the mutual-fund reservation, and the lock-in?
How is the NII bucket split into sHNI (₹2L–10L) and bHNI (>₹10L), when did that split take effect, and how does the draw of lots work within each sub-category?

What does retail allotment actually look like under the two cases the regulation distinguishes: undersubscribed retail (proportional, every applicant gets at least the minimum bid lot plus a proportional top-up) versus oversubscribed retail (the SEBI lottery — 1,75,000 out of 2,00,000 applicants from the worked example get the minimum lot; the rest get nothing, regardless of how many lots they bid for)?
How are employee and shareholder reservation portions carved out of the issue, and what are the caps (5% / ₹2L cap per employee with the under-subscription roll-up, 10% issue size for shareholders)?
What is the SEBI rule about compensation when your ASBA application fails through SCSB error and you miss the allotment?
must_not_say: Any advice or speculation about how to maximise allotment chances. The regulation makes this impossible by design (within the retail category, a one-lot application and a fourteen-lot application have identical odds in an oversubscribed issue). Do not hint otherwise.
Any prediction about which IPOs will be oversubscribed, or any 'tips' framing.
Any comparison to US/UK IPO allotment unless explicitly making the point that the Indian retail lottery is a deliberate fairness mechanism not present in those jurisdictions, and only if sourced.
Numbers, dates, or rule citations that are not directly supported by the source corpus excerpts. No phantom precision.
angle: Indian retail allotment is engineered to be a lottery, not a market. The article walks the reader through the actual mechanics — the categories, the percentages, the sub-splits, the draw of lots — using the verbatim worked example SEBI itself uses in Schedule XIII of the ICDR Regulations. The takeaway: applying for more does not help you, once the retail category is oversubscribed. The fairness of the lottery is the feature.
notes: Anchor article for the Academy. Two primary sources (consolidated ICDR Regulations 2018 as amended March 2025, and the Master Circular for ICDR consolidated November 2024). Both PDFs cached locally under data/academy/pdfs/. We may add secondary sources (specific IPO subscription numbers from Reuters/Mint) later if the outline finds a gap; for the first run we test whether the regulation-only corpus produces a publishable article.
